title: The suffering servant (Isaiah 53)
hookLine: despised, bruised for our sins, and by his bruises healed; read on Good Friday

lines: A CHARIOT ON A DESERT ROAD.
DO YOU UNDERSTAND WHAT YOU READ?
OF WHOM DOES THE PROPHET SPEAK?
cards: A man is riding home in a chariot on a desert road, reading aloud from a scroll of Isaiah. He's an official of the queen of Ethiopia, a long way from home after worshiping in Jerusalem. That's in the Acts of the Apostles.
A follower of Jesus named Philip runs up alongside and asks: do you understand what you're reading? How can I, the man says, unless someone guides me?
Then he asks what readers still ask about this chapter: of whom is the prophet saying this? Of himself, or of someone else?

teach.b: Isaiah's later chapters sing of a figure called the servant of the Lord, and in chapter fifty-three the servant suffers.
The Douay-Rheims: "Despised, and the most abject of men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity."
People turned their faces from him and thought God had struck him.

Then the voice in the poem realizes what was really happening: "he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our sins: the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruises we are healed."
They thought he was punished for his own wrongs. He was carrying theirs. "All we like sheep have gone astray."
And the servant doesn't fight back: like a lamb led to the slaughter, he opens not his mouth. Who is he? Readers answer in different ways.
Jewish tradition has often read the servant as the people of Israel, suffering among the nations, and some ancient Jewish readers saw a coming Messiah.
Christians, from the earliest days Acts records, have read it as Jesus. Philip begins from this very passage and tells the Ethiopian about Jesus, and at the next stream the man asks to be baptized.
The Catholic Church reads Isaiah fifty-three every Good Friday, as the first reading before the Passion.

teach.h: BY HIS BRUISES WE ARE HEALED.
teach.b: And that's week sixty: exile, Isaiah's here am I, Emmanuel, ploughshares, the wolf and the lamb, comfort, and the servant who carried what wasn't his.

how: On Good Friday, Catholics hear Isaiah 52:13–53:12 as the first reading of the Celebration of the Lord's Passion, before the Passion according to John and the veneration of the cross.

games.q: you're Philip, running beside the Ethiopian's chariot. he's reading Isaiah 53 and asks: of whom does the prophet say this? what do you do?
o: tell him it's too hard to explain.
say it's about the prophet himself.
begin from that very passage and tell him about Jesus.

practice: Bring to mind someone carrying a weight they didn't earn: a child in a hard home, someone wrongly accused, someone blamed for a family's troubles, someone sick because of where they live.
People looked away from the servant; for these minutes, don't look away from them. If you pray, bring them before God, and ask that they be seen and healed.

wordCard.voice: eved. Hebrew for servant: Isaiah's figure who is despised, bears the sins of others, and by whose bruises we are healed. Today's word.
